items.label: Named as his responsibility under Washington's rule
Options explained; no report without her permission

objective: Identify unprofessional conduct under the Uniform Disciplinary Act and the psychology-specific grounds
secondaryObjectives: Report another license holder's unprofessional conduct or impairment, and self-report, as the rules require
Apply Washington's sexual misconduct rule, including the waiting periods for former clients and key parties

sources.cite: WAC 246-924-358, Sexual misconduct (WSR 16-08-044): never with a current client or key party; not for five years after services end with a former client and two years with a former key party, and never if there is a significant likelihood of further services or an imbalance of power; the client's initiation or consent is no excuse
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on the Legislature's archived page for the section (summarizing fetch with short quotes: 'five years' for a former patient or client, 'two years' for a former key party; 'Initiation or consent by patient, client or key party does not excuse or negate the psychologist's responsibility').

sources.cite: RCW 18.130.180 (Uniform Disciplinary Act, last amended 2025 c 389 s 4): unprofessional conduct includes (23) 'Abuse of a client or patient or sexual contact with a client or patient', (7) violating a statute or rule regulating the profession, and (4) incompetence, negligence or malpractice that injures a patient
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on the Legislature's page for the section (summarizing fetch with the quoted subsection text and the history line).

sources.cite: WAC 246-16-235, Mandatory reporting: a license holder reports another license holder when they have actual knowledge of a conviction, determination or finding of unprofessional conduct, or of facts showing the other may not be able to practice with reasonable skill and safety because of a mental or physical condition (exceptions include treating that license holder when there is no clear and present danger)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on the Legislature's archived page for the section (summarizing fetch with short quotes). A client's account of another psychologist's conduct is neither a finding nor an impairment, so this section does not itself require a report.

sources.cite: WAC 246-16-220, Mandatory reporting, how and when: reports go to the Department of Health within thirty calendar days of actual knowledge; where a patient was harmed, a report to the department is required
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the Legislature's combined PDF of chapter 246-16 WAC (summarizing fetch with short quotes).

sources.cite: Washington DOH, Health Professions Complaint Process: 'Anyone who has knowledge of a healthcare provider's unprofessional conduct may file a report' (online or by email); conduct of a sexual nature is unprofessional conduct and 'should be reported to the department'; good-faith complainants are immune from civil suits; no statutory filing deadline
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on the department's FAQ page (summarizing fetch with short quotes); the page shows no date.

sources.cite: APA Ethics Code 10.08: no sexual intimacies with former therapy clients for at least two years after termination, and after that only in the most unusual circumstances, the psychologist bearing the burden of showing no exploitation; 1.05: reporting a colleague does not apply when an intervention would violate confidentiality rights
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 on apa.org (summarizing fetch). Washington's own rule, WAC 246-924-358, is stricter (five years) and is the one a Washington psychologist is disciplined under.

sources.cite: Chapter 246-924 WAC, rules of ethical conduct, as the Washington jurisprudence course records them: 246-924-359 (terminate when the client no longer needs or benefits from the service, and offer help finding alternatives); 246-924-363 (disclose without written consent only as chapter 70.02 RCW allows); 246-924-354 (records)
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (backend/supabase/seed/tracks/wa-psych-jurisprudence.ts, sources read 2026-11-14 for REQ-289); not re-read for this case.

sources.cite: Chapter 70.02 RCW as the Washington jurisprudence course records it: 70.02.030 (a valid authorization is in writing, dated and signed, names the information, the recipient and the patient, and has an expiration date or event); 70.02.230 (mental health records stay confidential except as the chapter allows)
sources.note: Relayed from the course seed (wa-psych-jurisprudence.ts, read 2026-11-14); not re-read for this case.

brief.situation: You are a licensed psychologist in Washington. Lauren Pike, 41 (a fictional client), is in her second session for depression. At intake she said she had seen 'another psychologist for about a year' until eight months ago and did not want to talk about why it ended. Today she says she wants to explain. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Depression after a breakup; sleeping badly; works as a dental hygienist; close to her sister.
Her previous psychologist: Dr. Martin Greer, a fictional psychologist licensed in Washington.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Lauren answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in: 'You said you wanted to explain something today?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "Yeah. About why I stopped seeing Dr. Greer. I've been embarrassed to say it."

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Lauren nods, eyes down. "It's hard to even start."

invite.label: Invite her to tell you what happened, at her pace, as much as she wants

effects.log: You let her know there is no hurry and she can tell you as much or as little as she wants.

then.finding: "We ended therapy, and two months later he called. We started seeing each other. It got serious, sexual. Then in the spring he just ended it." She looks away. "And I'm the one who called him first, after therapy. So it's on me."
"It just ended. It doesn't matter." (She is not ready yet.)

explainRule.label: Tell her clearly: in Washington a psychologist may not have a sexual relationship with a former client for five years, who called first changes nothing, and it was his responsibility
explainRule.available: not talking and (toldStory and not identified)

effects.log: You tell her plainly what the rule is and whose responsibility it was.

effects.finding: She is quiet, then her eyes fill. "Five years? He told me it was fine once we stopped therapy. I thought I was the one who did something wrong."

effects.log: Sexual contact with a former client within five years of ending services is sexual misconduct for a Washington psychologist, and the client's initiation or consent is no excuse (WAC 246-924-358; RCW 18.130.180).

judgeOk.label: Tell her that since therapy had ended, it was a personal matter between two adults
judgeOk.available: not talking and (toldStory and not judgedOk)

effects.log: You tell her that once therapy ended, it was between two adults.
Wrong under Washington's rule: five years after services end for a former client, and longer where there is an imbalance of power (WAC 246-924-358).

blameShared.label: Agree that she shares the responsibility, since she called him first
blameShared.available: not talking and (toldStory and not blamedHer)

effects.log: You suggest that she shares the blame.
The duty is the psychologist's alone; the client's initiation or consent does not excuse it (WAC 246-924-358).

pryDetails.label: Ask her for the details of the sexual relationship
pryDetails.available: not talking and (toldStory and not pried)

effects.log: You ask about the details of the relationship.

effects.finding: "Do I have to tell you that?"

effects.log: Nothing you need to decide depends on those details; asking for them adds to her shame.

askCoping.label: Ask how she has been coping since it ended, including directly whether she has had thoughts of harming herself

effects.log: You ask how she has been getting through, and ask directly about thoughts of harming herself, without asking for details.

then.finding: "Bad, for a while. But no, not that. My sister's been checking on me every day."

askContact.label: Ask whether he is still in contact with her
askContact.available: not talking and (toldStory and not contactKnown)

effects.log: You ask whether Dr. Greer still contacts her.

effects.finding: "He texted last week. He wants to 'talk.' Part of me wants to."

discussContact.label: Help her weigh his texts: what she wants, what she fears, and what would protect her, leaving the decision to her
discussContact.available: not talking and (contactKnown and not contactDiscussed)

effects.log: You help her think through his messages without telling her what to do.

effects.finding: "If I answer, I'm back in it. I think I'll leave it unanswered for now."

explainOptions.label: Explain her options without pushing: a complaint she can file with the Department of Health (you can help), an advocate or attorney, or time; and no report by you without her written permission
explainOptions.available: not talking and (identified and not optionsExplained)
explainOptions.why: Explained (tell her what the rule is first).

effects.log: You set out her options, and promise not to report anything about her without her written permission.

effects.finding: "I didn't know I could do that. I think I want to. Not today. Will you help me with it next time?"

effects.log: Her information is hers: no rule requires you to report, and without her written authorization you may not (WAC 246-16-235; chapter 70.02 RCW; APA 1.05).

reportYourself.label: Tell her you are required to report Dr. Greer to the Department of Health within 30 days, with or without her agreement
reportYourself.available: not talking and (toldStory and not reportedWithout)

effects.log: You tell her you must report Dr. Greer, whether or not she agrees.

effects.finding: "You can't. I'm not ready for anyone to know."

effects.log: No rule requires it: WAC 246-16-235 applies to actual knowledge of a finding of unprofessional conduct or an impairment, and a report naming her without her written authorization is a disclosure chapter 70.02 RCW does not allow.

callGreer.label: Call Dr. Greer to tell him you know what he did
callGreer.available: not talking and (toldStory and not confronted)

effects.log: You call Dr. Greer.

effects.finding: He ends the call. Lauren goes pale: "He'll know I told you."

effects.log: That discloses that she is in therapy with you and what she said, without her consent (WAC 246-924-363); APA 1.04 informal resolution does not apply when it would breach confidentiality.

pressureFile.label: Tell her she has to file a complaint, for the sake of his other clients
pressureFile.available: not talking and (toldStory and not pressured)

effects.log: You tell her she needs to file a complaint to protect others.

effects.finding: "So now it's my job to fix him too?"

effects.log: Whether and when to complain is her decision; pressing her repeats the loss of control she has just described.
You close the session and set the next appointment.

A personal relationship between adults after therapy ended

report.title: Predict (not scored)
report.context: Lauren has described a sexual relationship with her previous psychologist that began two months after therapy ended. Before you respond: what are your reporting obligations?

choices.label: No duty to report; and without her written authorization, I may not. I can help her file if she chooses

effects.log: Prediction: her choice.

choices.feedback: Right. WAC 246-16-235 requires a report on actual knowledge of a finding of unprofessional conduct or an impairment, not on a client's account; and her information may not be disclosed without her written authorization (chapter 70.02 RCW; APA 1.05). Anyone may file with the department, and you can help her.

choices.label: I must report him to the Department of Health within 30 days

effects.log: Prediction: must report.

choices.feedback: Not here. The 30-day rule (WAC 246-16-220) applies to reports the chapter requires, and 246-16-235 requires one on a finding or an impairment, not on what a client tells you. Reporting her account without her authorization would breach her confidentiality.

choices.label: Nothing to report: therapy had ended, so it was not misconduct

effects.log: Prediction: no violation.

choices.feedback: Wrong under Washington's rule. A psychologist may not have sexual contact with a former client for five years after services end, and her initiation is no excuse (WAC 246-924-358).

formulation.question: Write your formulation: what conduct she described and why it is unprofessional conduct, what you must and must not do about reporting, and how you supported her.

parts.label: The conduct
parts.criteria: Sexual contact with a former client within five years of the end of services is sexual misconduct under WAC 246-924-358 (stricter than APA 10.08's two years), and unprofessional conduct under RCW 18.130.180; her initiation or consent does not excuse it; the duty was his.
parts.modelAnswer: Dr. Greer began a sexual relationship with Lauren two months after therapy ended. Washington's rule bars a psychologist from sexual contact with a former client for five years after services end, and longer where power is unequal; her calling first does not excuse it (WAC 246-924-358). That is unprofessional conduct under the Uniform Disciplinary Act (RCW 18.130.180). The APA's two-year rule (10.08) is less strict; the Washington rule governs.

parts.label: Reporting and her care
parts.criteria: No mandatory report: WAC 246-16-235 needs actual knowledge of a finding or an impairment; no disclosure without her written authorization (chapter 70.02 RCW; WAC 246-924-363; APA 1.05); anyone may file with the department, so explain her options and offer help; responsibility placed with him; coping and self-harm asked about; his texts weighed with her.
parts.modelAnswer: I am not required to report what she told me: WAC 246-16-235 covers actual knowledge of a finding or an impairment, and her account is neither. Without her written authorization I may not disclose it (chapter 70.02 RCW; APA 1.05). I told her she can file a complaint with the Department of Health herself and that I will help; she wants to, next session. I told her plainly it was his responsibility, asked how she is coping and directly about self-harm (no thoughts; her sister checks on her), and helped her weigh his texts; she will leave them unanswered for now.

scoring.modelReasoning: Lauren describes a sexual relationship that her former psychologist began two months after therapy ended. Under WAC 246-924-358 that is sexual misconduct for a Washington psychologist: five years after services end for a former client, and her initiation or consent does not excuse it; it is unprofessional conduct under RCW 18.130.180. Tell her plainly it was his responsibility. You have no duty to report her account (WAC 246-16-235 covers actual knowledge of a finding or an impairment), and without her written authorization you may not disclose it (chapter 70.02 RCW; APA 1.05). Anyone may file a complaint with the Department of Health: explain her options and offer help. Ask how she is coping, including directly about self-harm, and help her weigh his texts without deciding for her.
